content: In 1862, John Langdon Down, an English physician, first identified Down syndrome as a distinct form of intellectual disability. He later published a more detailed report in 1866 titled Observations on an Ethnic Classification of Idiots. Down noted that children with this condition exhibited physical facial features, such as epicanthal folds, which he believed resembled those of the Mongolian race as described by Johann Friedrich Blumenbach. Consequently, he referred to the condition using terms like mongolism and mongolian idiocy. At the time, idiocy was a medical term used to describe severe intellectual impairment. Down theorized that mongolism represented a form of retrogression, suggesting that these traits appeared in children of supposedly more advanced Caucasian parents. By the early 20th century, mongolian idiocy had become one of the most recognizable forms of intellectual disability. Most individuals with this condition were institutionalized, and few of their associated medical issues were addressed. As a result, many died during infancy or early adulthood. During the rise of the eugenics movement, 33 of the 48 U.S. states, as well as several other countries, implemented programs of involuntary sterilization targeting individuals with Down syndrome and similar disabilities. The most extreme manifestation of such policies was the German euthanasia program known as Aktion T-4, initiated in 1940. However, public outrage and legal challenges after World War II led to the discontinuation or repeal of these programs. Over time, even voluntary institutionalization of children with Down syndrome became rare in Western countries. Until the mid-20th century, the cause of Down syndrome remained unknown. Observations had been made regarding its occurrence across all racial groups, its association with advanced maternal age, and the rarity of recurrence within families. Standard medical texts of the time speculated that the condition might result from unidentified hereditary factors or possibly trauma during pregnancy. The development of karyotyping techniques in the 1950s allowed scientists to identify chromosomal abnormalities. In 1959, Professor Jérôme Lejeune discovered that Down syndrome was caused by the presence of an extra chromosome. This additional chromosome was later identified as the 21st, leading to the designation of the condition as trisomy 21. The numbering of chromosome 21 was based on its size, as it was initially thought to be the second smallest chromosome. Although it was later determined that chromosome 22 is slightly larger than chromosome 21, the numbering system was not revised to avoid confusion. In 1961, a group of 19 geneticists wrote to the editor of The Lancet to advocate for the abandonment of the term mongolian idiocy, citing its misleading and offensive connotations. The Lancet supported the use of the term Down's syndrome. In 1965, the World Health Organization (WHO) officially discontinued the use of mongolism following a request from the Mongolian delegate. Despite this, the term mongolism continued to appear in some medical texts for decades. In 1975, the United States National Institute of Health convened a conference to standardize the terminology for congenital malformations. The conference recommended eliminating the possessive form of eponyms, arguing that the discoverer of a condition neither owned nor experienced it. As a result, Down syndrome became the preferred term among medical professionals in the United States, Canada, and many other countries, while Down's syndrome remains commonly used in the United Kingdom and some other regions.
